newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE-China uses Hong Kong to whip up patriotism.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-China uses Hong Kong to whip up patriotism.

text.p: For students at the elite Beijing 80th High School, the return of Hong Kong to Chinese rule in July after more than 150 years of British colonial rule is about patriotism, power, pride and prejudice.
"We are using the return of Hong Kong to teach our students to be patriotic," school assistant principal Yao Dianyun said in an interview.

Chinese authorities are finding Hong Kong a potent symbol in their drive to use patriotism to stop a slide in public confidence in the corruption-plagued Communist Party that has ruled China since 1949.
"We tell our students to love the country...and make the motherland rich and strong," Yao said.
"If a country is weak, it'll take a beating," Yao said.

A series of beatings that China is eager to put behind it are the 19th-century "Opium Wars" in which Britain seized Hong Kong after defeating the armies of the Qing dynasty (1644-1911) emperors and winning the right to export opium to China.

Britain agreed in 1984 to return Hong Kong to China at midnight on June 30 this year under a "one country, two systems" formula, in which China promises the territory can keep its capitalist lifestyle and enjoy a high degree of autonomy for 50 years after the handover.
The return of Hong Kong is seen by many Chinese as righting a wrong that humiliated a proud nation -- the "Middle Kingdom" as China is known in Chinese -- and one of the world's oldest civilisations.
"Foreigners have unceasingly bullied China for more than 150 years," said Liu Shuyong, a fellow at the institute of modern history of the prestigious Chinese Academy of Social Sciences.
The return of Hong Kong can wipe out more than a century of disgrace, many Chinese believe.
"This (Hong Kong) is ours. We must get it back," Liu said.

For Lin Dong, a 16-year-old student at Beijing 80th High School, the handover is evidence that "power comes from the barrel of the gun" as the late Chairman Mao Zedong quipped -- and young Chinese such as Lin are now confident that China wields power.
"Now that China is strong, Britain does not dare not to return Hong Kong to China," Lin said after a lecture at his school on the significance of the return of Hong Kong.
"I'm proud to be a Chinese," he said.
Zhang Tao, a 31-year-old teacher, couldn't agree more. "Hong Kong's return is inevitable now that China is strong."
An hour-long lecture by Zhang began with a rendition by the class of a Chinese song about Hong Kong -- "Pearl of the Orient" -- Hong Kong's nickname in Chinese.

"We must not forget...the humiliation," Zhang told an audience of about 50 students against a backdrop of a map of the enclave, drawings of Hong Kong's regional flag and emblem and a huge photograph giving a bird's-eye view of the territory.
In the last days before China wipes away at least this colonial-era humiliation, the return of Hong Kong has become an obsession at the school -- as in much of the rest of China.
The auditorium was decorated with calligraphy, poems, paintings and embroideries marking Hong Kong's handover.

Also on display were photos of the People's Liberation Army soldiers who will be stationed in Hong Kong after the handover -- and Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin shaking hands with Hong Kong's future leader, Tung Chee-hwa.
A board counting down the number of days before Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule greets visitors near the school's gate.
Banners bearing patriotic slogans and propaganda are strung around the school. "Remember 100 years of history. Stir up patriotic sentiments. Determined to build a strong nation," one read.

The Beijing 80th High School is gearing up for the handover with a contest on how much students know about Hong Kong. Many have become walking encyclopaedias on the tiny territory after spending countless hours studying its history.
Some have learnt prejudice as well as pride, regarding Britain's colonial rule as a century and a half of harm.

"Hong Kong is prosperous...due mainly to the hard work of Hong Kong Chinese themselves, the mainland backing it and its geographical location," said Sun Yu, a first year senior high school student. He ignored mention of Britain's contributions.
"Hong Kong is a money tree for Britain," said the academic, Liu.
He attributed Hong Kong's success while in British hands to the tolerance of the late Chairman Mao Zedong and his decision not to take Hong Kong after the communists swept to power.
"The People's Liberation Army was perfectly capable of taking Hong Kong then...British resistance would have been futile," Liu said.
But many Chinese believe they really have Mao's successor to thank for the recovery of Hong Kong.
"Mao Zedong is great because he unified the country. Deng Xiaoping is great because he recovered Hong Kong," a Chinese writer said.
